      G3-01 After a consumer notifies a financial institution of an electronic fund transfer error, what investigation and resolution steps are required, and within what time limits?                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           # Electronic Fund Transfer Error Investigation and Resolution Requirements\n\n## 1. Triggering a Valid Notice of Error\n\nA financial institution must comply with error resolution procedures when it receives an oral or written notice of error that [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0001]:\n\n- Is received **no later than 60 days** after the institution sends the periodic statement on which the alleged error is first reflected;\n- Enables the institution to identify the **consumer's name and account number**; and\n- Indicates **why the consumer believes an error exists**, including to the extent possible the type, date, and amount of the error.\n\nThe institution may require the consumer to provide **written confirmation within 10 business days** of an oral notice. If it does, it must inform the consumer of this requirement and provide the address for sending confirmation [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n## 2. Standard Investigation Timeline: 10-Business-Day Period\n\nAfter receiving a valid notice of error, the financial institution must [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002]:\n\n1. **Investigate promptly** and determine whether an error occurred **within 10 business days** of receiving the notice.\n2. **Report results to the consumer within 3 business days** after completing the investigation.\n3. **Correct the error within 1 business day** after determining that an error occurred.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Extended Investigation Timeline: 45-Calendar-Day Period\n\nIf the institution **cannot complete its investigation within 10 business days**, it may take **up to 45 days** from receipt of the notice, provided it does **all** of the following [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002]:\n\n1. **Provisionally credits** the consumer's account in the full amount of the alleged error (including interest where applicable) **within 10 business days** of receiving the error notice.\n   - If the institution has a reasonable basis for believing an unauthorized EFT occurred and has satisfied § 1005.6(a) requirements, it may **withhold up to $50** from the provisional credit.\n2. **Informs the consumer within 2 business days** after the provisional crediting of the amount and date of the credit, and gives the consumer **full use of the funds** during the investigation.\n3. **Corrects the error within 1 business day** after determining that an error occurred.\n4. **Reports results to the consumer within 3 business days** after completing the investigation, including notice that a provisional credit has been made final (if applicable).\n\n### Exceptions — No Provisional Credit Required:\nThe institution need **not** provisionally credit the account (and thus may still take up to 45 days) if [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002]:\n- The institution required but **did not receive written confirmation** within 10 business days of an oral notice; **or**\n- The alleged error involves an account subject to **Regulation T** (Securities Credit by Brokers and Dealers, 12 CFR Part 220).\n\n---\n\n## 4. Further Extended Time Periods\n\nCertain circumstances extend the standard deadlines [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0702_chunk_0001]:\n\n| Circumstance | Standard Period | Extended Period |\n|---|---|---|\n| EFT occurred within **30 days after first deposit** to the account | 10 business days | **20 business days** |\n| EFT occurred within **30 days after first deposit** (45-day extended period) | 45 days | **90 days** |\n| EFT **not initiated within a state** | 45 days | **90 days** |\n| EFT resulted from a **point-of-sale debit card transaction** | 45 days | **90 days** |\n\n---\n\n## 5. Scope of Investigation\n\nA financial institution's review of **its own records** satisfies the investigation requirement if [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0003]:\n- The alleged error concerns a transfer **to or from a third party**; **and**\n- There is **no agreement** between the institution and the third party for the type of EFT involved.\n\nHowever, the institution **may not limit its investigation solely to payment instructions** where other records pertaining to the account may help resolve the consumer's claim [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0701_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n## 6. If the Institution Determines No Error (or a Different Error) Occurred\n\nThe institution must [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0003] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0701_chunk_0001]:\n\n1. **Mail or deliver a written explanation** of its findings **within 3 business days** after concluding the investigation.\n2. Include in the explanation a **notice of the consumer's right to request the documents** relied upon in making the determination.\n3. **Promptly provide copies** of those documents upon the consumer's request.\n\n### If Provisional Credit Was Granted and Is Now Being Debited Back:\nThe institution must [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0003] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0702_chunk_0001]:\n- **Notify the consumer** of the date and amount of the debiting.\n- **Honor checks, drafts, or similar instruments** payable to third parties and preauthorized transfers from the consumer's account (without overdraft charge) for **5 business days** after the notification — but only items it would have paid had the provisional credit not been debited.\n\n---\n\n## 7. The financial institution may take up to 45 calendar days (12 CFR 1005.11(c)(2)) to complete its investigation provided it: • Provisionally credits the funds (including interest, where applicable) to the consumer’s account within the 10 business-day period. • Advises the consumer within two business days of the provisional crediting. • Gives the consumer full use of the funds during the investigation. A financial institution need not provisionally credit the account to take up to 45 calendar days to complete its investigation if the consumer fails to provide the required written confirmation of an oral notice of error, or if the notice of error involves an account subject to the margin requirements or other aspects of Regulation T (Securities Credit by Brokers and Dealers, 12 CFR Part 220) (12 CFR 1005.11(c)(2)(i)(B)). However, where an error involves an unauthorized EFT, the financial institution must comply with the requirements of the provisions relating to unauthorized EFTs before holding the consumer liable, even if the consumer does not provide a notice of error within the time limits in 12 CFR 1005.11(b) (Comment 1005.11(b)(1)-7). When investigating a claim of error, the financial institution need only review its own records if the alleged error concerns a transfer to or from a third party, and there is no agreement between the financial institution and the third party for the type of EFT involved (12 CFR 1005.11(c)(4)). However, the financial institution may not limit its investigation solely to the payment instructions where other information within the financial institution’s records pertaining to a particular account may help to resolve a consumer’s claim (Comment 1005.11(c)(4)-5). If, after investigating the alleged error, the financial institution determines that an error has occurred, it must promptly (within one business day after such determination) correct the error, including the crediting of interest if applicable. The financial institution must provide within three business days of the completed investigation an oral or written report of the correction to the consumer and, as applicable, notify the consumer that the provisional credit has been made final (12 CFR 1005.11(c)(2)(iii) and (iv)). If the financial institution determines that no error occurred or that an error occurred in a different manner or amount from that described by the consumer, the financial institution must mail or deliver a written explanation of its findings within three business days after concluding its investigation.                                                                                                                                                             ## Liability Limits for Lost or Stolen Access Devices Under Regulation E\n\n### Threshold Conditions for Any Liability\n\nBefore a consumer can be held liable at all, certain conditions must be satisfied. Under 12 CFR 1005.6(a), a consumer may be held liable for an unauthorized EFT only if the financial institution has provided the disclosures required by § 1005.7(b)(1), (2), and (3) — specifically: a summary of consumer liability, the telephone number and address for reporting, and the institution's business days. If the unauthorized transfer involved an access device, it must be an **accepted** access device, and the financial institution must have provided **a means to identify** the consumer to whom the device was issued [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\nRegulation E expressly **prohibits** using consumer negligence (e.g., writing a PIN on an ATM card) or a deposit agreement as a basis for imposing greater liability than the limits set forth in § 1005.6(b). The extent of the consumer's liability is determined solely by the consumer's promptness in notifying the financial institution [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0697_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### Tiered Liability Structure for Loss or Theft of an Access Device\n\nThe first two tiers under 12 CFR 1005.6(b)(1) and (b)(2) apply **only when an access device is lost or stolen**. They do not apply to unauthorized transfers made without an access device (see the separate rule below) [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0728_chunk_0001].\n\n#### Tier 1 — § 1005.6(b)(1): Notice Given Within Two Business Days of Learning of Loss or Theft\n\n- **Maximum liability:** The **lesser of $50** or the total amount of unauthorized transfers that occur before notice is given to the financial institution [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\nPer CFPB examination checklist guidance, examiners verify that the institution limits liability to this amount when the consumer notifies within the two-business-day window [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0727_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n#### Tier 2 — § 1005.6(b)(2): Notice NOT Given Within Two Business Days (but within 60 calendar days of statement transmittal)\n\n- **Maximum liability:** The **lesser of $500** or the **sum of**:\n  - (a) $50 **or** the amount of unauthorized transfers occurring within the first two business days, **whichever is less**; **AND**\n  - (b) The amount of unauthorized transfers occurring **after** the close of two business days and **before** notice to the institution — *provided the institution establishes that these transfers would not have occurred had the consumer notified the institution within the two-day period* [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\nPer CFPB examination checklist guidance, examiners verify that the institution does not exceed this cap when the consumer fails to notify within two business days [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0727_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n#### Tier 3 — § 1005.6(b)(3): Failure to Report Within 60 Calendar Days of Periodic Statement Transmittal\n\nThis rule applies to **all** unauthorized EFTs appearing on a periodic statement — whether or not an access device was involved — and operates separately from Tiers 1 and 2 [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\nUnder 12 CFR 1005.6(b)(3), a consumer must report an unauthorized electronic fund transfer that appears on a periodic statement **within 60 calendar days** of the institution's transmittal of that statement to avoid liability for subsequent transfers. If the consumer **fails** to do so, the consumer's liability shall not exceed the amount of unauthorized transfers occurring **after** the close of the 60-day period and **before** notice to the institution, provided the institution establishes that those transfers would not have occurred had timely notice been given [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\nWhen an **access device** is involved in the unauthorized transfer, the consumer may **also** be liable for amounts set forth in § 1005.6(b)(1) or (b)(2), as applicable [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\n**Late reporting when an access device is involved — distinction between transfer timing:** CFPB examination guidance further clarifies that when a consumer reports more than 60 calendar days after transmittal of the statement showing the first unauthorized transfer made with an access device, the liability analysis distinguishes between two categories of transfers:\n\n- For unauthorized transfers occurring **within** the 60-day period: liability is capped at the lesser of $500, or the sum of (a) the lesser of $50 or the amount of unauthorized transfers in the first two business days, and (b) the amount of unauthorized transfers occurring after two business days (subject to the institution's burden of proof); and\n- For unauthorized transfers occurring **after** the 60-day period: the consumer faces **unlimited liability** until the financial institution is notified, provided the institution demonstrates those transfers would not have occurred had timely notice been given [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001].\n\nCFPB examination checklist guidance confirms: if the consumer notifies within 60 days, the institution may not hold the consumer liable for transfers occurring after the 60-day period; if the consumer does not notify within 60 days, liability is limited to transfers occurring after the 60-day period and before notice, subject to the institution's burden of proof [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0728_chunk_0001].\n\n> **Important distinction (CFPB examination checklist guidance):** The first two tiers of liability under § 1005.6(b)(1) and (b)(2) do **not** apply to unauthorized transfers from a consumer's account made **without** an access device. Only the 60-day rule under § 1005.6(b)(3) governs such transfers [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0728_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### Special Rule: Unauthorized Transfers NOT Involving an Access Device\n\nWhere an unauthorized transfer occurs **without** the loss or theft of an access device (e.g., account number compromise without a card), the tiered $50/$500 structure of § 1005.6(b)(1) and (b)(2) does **not** apply. Instead, only the 60-day periodic statement rule under § 1005.6(b)(3) governs. CFPB examination guidance summarizes the outcomes for this scenario as follows:\n\n| Timing of Consumer Notice | Maximum Liability |\n|---|---|\n| Within 60 calendar days after transmittal of the periodic statement on which the unauthorized transfer first appears | No liability for unauthorized transfers occurring after the 60-day period |\n| More than 60 calendar days after transmittal of the periodic statement on which the unauthorized transfer first appears | Unlimited liability for unauthorized transfers occurring after the 60-day period and before notice to the financial institution (provided the institution establishes the transfers would not have occurred had timely notice been given) |\n\n[C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0728_chunk_0001]\n\nNote that the "no liability" characterization in the table above reflects CFPB examination guidance summarizing the practical outcome; the text of 12 CFR 1005.6(b)(3) itself frames the rule in terms of what liability the consumer incurs for transfers occurring *after* the close of the 60-day period [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### Extension of Time Limits for Extenuating Circumstances\n\nIf the consumer's delay in notifying the financial institution was due to **extenuating circumstances** (e.g., extended travel or hospitalization), the institution **must extend** the applicable time periods — including the two-business-day and 60-day periods — to a **reasonable period** [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0699_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### How Notice Is Given\n\n- Notice is effective when the consumer **takes steps reasonably necessary** to provide the institution with pertinent information, whether or not a particular employee actually receives it [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n- At the consumer's option, notice may be given **in person, by telephone, or in writing** [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0699_chunk_0001].\n- Written notice is considered given at the time of mailing or delivery for transmission [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0699_chunk_0001].\n- Notice may also be considered given when the institution becomes aware of circumstances leading to a reasonable belief that an unauthorized transfer has been or may be made [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0699_chunk_0001].\n- The consumer need not provide the account or card number; sufficiently identifying the account (e.g., name and account type) is enough [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0699_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### Special Rule: Service Providers Without Account-Holding Agreements\n\nWhere a service provider issues a debit card but does not hold the consumer's account and has no agreement with the account-holding institution, the **two-business-day notice period under § 1005.6(b)(1) and (b)(2) is extended to four business days**, and the **60-day reporting period under § 1005.6(b)(3) is extended to 90 days** [C:12CFR1005_1005.14_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### Reduced Liability by Agreement or State Law\n\nA financial institution **may impose less** consumer liability than the statutory limits based on state law or the deposit agreement [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### Summary Table\n\n| Scenario | Timing of Consumer Notice | Maximum Liability |\n|---|---|---|\n| Loss/theft of access device — § 1005.6(b)(1) | Within 2 business days of learning of loss/theft | Lesser of **$50** or actual unauthorized transfers before notice |\n| Loss/theft of access device — § 1005.6(b)(2) | More than 2 business days after learning of loss/theft, up to 60 days after statement | Lesser of **$500** or sum of (a) lesser of $50 or transfers in first 2 days, plus (b) transfers after 2 days and before notice (institution must prove causation) |\n| Loss/theft of access device — more than 60 days after statement | More than 60 calendar days after transmittal of statement showing first unauthorized transfer | For transfers within the 60-day period: lesser of $500 per (b)(2) calculation; for transfers after the 60-day period: **unlimited** (until notice; institution must prove causation) |\n| Any unauthorized EFT on periodic statement — § 1005.6(b)(3) (access device or not) | Within 60 calendar days after statement transmittal | **No additional liability** for post-60-day transfers |\n| Any unauthorized EFT on periodic statement — § 1005.6(b)(3) (access device or not) | More than 60 calendar days after statement transmittal | **Unlimited** for transfers after the 60-day period and before notice (institution must prove causation); if access device involved, also subject to (b)(1)/(b)(2) amounts for transfers within the 60-day period |\n| Unauthorized transfer **without** access device | Within 60 days of statement | No liability for post-60-day transfers (per CFPB examination guidance) |\n| Unauthorized transfer **without** access device | More than 60 days after statement | Unlimited for post-60-day transfers and before notice (institution must prove causation) |\n\n[C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0728_chunk_0001]                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       [{"chunk_id": "exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001", "source": "exam_manual_v2_2012.pdf", "page": "", "rrf_score": 0.03252247488101534, "text": "CFPB Consumer Laws and Regulations EFTA those time limits, are listed in the chart below. Consumer Liability and Error Resolution Liability of Consumers for Unauthorized Transfers – 12 CFR 1005.6 A consumer may be liable for an unauthorized EFT (defined in 12 CFR 1005.2(m)) depending on when the consumer notifies the financial institution and whether an access device was used to conduct the transaction. Under the EFTA, there is no bright-line time limit within which consumers must report unauthorized EFTs (71 Fed. Reg. 1638, 1653 (Jan. 10, 2006)). The extent of the consumer’s liability is determined solely by the consumer’s promptness in notifying the financial institution (Comment 1005.6(b)-3). Other factors may not be used as a basis to hold consumers liable. Regulation E expressly prohibits the following factors as the basis for imposing greater liability than is permissible under Regulation E: the consumer was negligent (e.g., wrote a PIN on an ATM card); an agreement between the consumer and the financial institution provides for greater liability; or the consumer is liable for a greater amount under state law (Comments 1005.6(b)-2 and 1005.6(b)-3). A consumer may only be held liable for an unauthorized transaction, within the limitations set forth in 12 CFR 1005.6(b), if: • The financial institution has provided all of the following written disclosures to the consumer: o A summary of the consumer’s liability for unauthorized EFTs. o The telephone number and address for reporting that an unauthorized EFT has been or may be made. o The financial institution’s business days. • Any access device used to affect the EFT was an accepted access device (as defined in 12 CFR 1005.2(a)). • The financial institution has provided a means to identify the consumer to whom the access device was issued (12 CFR 1005.6(a)). Regulation E allows, but does not require, the financial institution to provide a separate means to identify each consumer of a multiple-user account (Comment 1005.6(a)-2). A consumer's liability for an unauthorized electronic fund transfer or a series of related unauthorized transfers shall be determined as follows: (1) Timely notice given. (4) Extension of time limits. If the consumer's delay in notifying the financial institution was due to extenuating circumstances, the institution shall extend the times specified above to a reasonable period.                                                                                                  # Initial Disclosures for Electronic Fund Transfer Services\n\n## Timing of Disclosures\n\nA financial institution must provide initial disclosures **at the time a consumer contracts for an electronic fund transfer service or before the first electronic fund transfer is made involving the consumer's account** [C:12CFR1005_1005.7_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0685_chunk_0001].\n\n**Key timing rules and exceptions:**\n\n- Disclosures given earlier than required (e.g., when a consumer opens a checking account) need not be repeated when the consumer later authorizes an electronic check conversion or agrees with a third party to initiate preauthorized transfers, **unless the terms and conditions differ** from those previously disclosed [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0685_chunk_0001].\n- Where the agreement for EFT services is directly between the consumer and the account-holding institution, disclosures must be given **in close proximity to the event requiring disclosure** (e.g., when the consumer contracts for a new service) [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0685_chunk_0001].\n- Where a consumer authorizes a third party to debit or credit the account and the institution has not received advance notice, the institution must provide disclosures **as soon as reasonably possible after the first debit or credit**, unless previously given [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0685_chunk_0001].\n- If a consumer opens a new account permitting EFTs and has already received Regulation E disclosures for another account at the same institution, the institution **need only disclose terms and conditions that differ** from those previously given [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0685_chunk_0001].\n- If a financial institution joins an interchange or shared network, disclosures are required for additional EFT services not previously available if the terms and conditions differ from those previously disclosed [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0685_chunk_0002].\n\n---\n\n## Required Content of Initial Disclosures (12 CFR 1005.7(b))\n\nThe following disclosures must be provided **as applicable** [C:12CFR1005_1005.7_chunk_0001]:\n\n### 1. Consumer Liability for Unauthorized Transfers\nA summary of the consumer's liability under § 1005.6, or under state or other applicable law or agreement, for unauthorized electronic fund transfers. A financial institution does not need to provide this disclosure if it imposes no liability, but must provide it before imposing any liability in the future [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0686_chunk_0001] [C:12CFR1005_1005.7_chunk_0001].\n\n### 2. Telephone Number and Address\nThe telephone number and address of the person or office to be notified when the consumer believes an unauthorized EFT has been or may be made. A **specific** telephone number and address must be provided for reporting a lost or stolen access device or a possible unauthorized transfer [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0686_chunk_0001] [C:12CFR1005_1005.7_chunk_0001].\n\n### 3. Business Days\nThe financial institution's business days [C:12CFR1005_1005.7_chunk_0001].\n\n### 4. Types of Transfers and Limitations on Frequency or Dollar Amount\nThe types of EFTs the consumer may make and any limitations on the frequency and dollar amount of transfers. Limitations generally must be disclosed in detail; however, **if confidentiality of certain details is essential to the security of an account or system, those details may be withheld**, but the existence of limitations must still be disclosed. A limitation on account activity that restricts the consumer's ability to make EFTs must be disclosed even if the restriction also applies to non-electronic transfers [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0686_chunk_0001] [C:12CFR1005_1005.7_chunk_0001].\n\n### 5. Fees\nAny fees imposed by the financial institution for EFTs or for the right to make transfers. A per-item fee must be disclosed even if the same fee applies to non-electronic transfers. If a fee applies only under certain conditions, those conditions must be disclosed [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0687_chunk_0001] [C:12CFR1005_1005.7_chunk_0001].\n\n### 6. Documentation\nA summary of the consumer's right to receipts and periodic statements (under § 1005.9), and notices regarding preauthorized transfers (under § 1005.10(a) and (d)) [C:12CFR1005_1005.7_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0687_chunk_0001].\n\n### 7. Stop Payment\nA summary of the consumer's right to stop payment of a preauthorized EFT and the procedure for placing a stop-payment order, as provided in § 1005.10(c) [C:12CFR1005_1005.7_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0687_chunk_0001].\n\n### 8. Liability of the Institution\nA summary of the financial institution's liability to the consumer under Section 910 of the EFTA for failure to make or to stop certain transfers [C:12CFR1005_1005.7_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0687_chunk_0001].\n\n### 9. Confidentiality\nThe circumstances under which, in the ordinary course of business, the financial institution may provide information concerning the consumer's account to third parties. This includes any information relating to an account to or from which EFTs are permitted, not just information about the EFTs themselves. Third parties include other subsidiaries of the same holding company [C:12CFR1005_1005.7_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0687_chunk_0001].\n\n### 10. Error Resolution\nA notice **substantially similar to Model Form A-3** as set out in Appendix A of Part 1005. Different wording may be used so long as the substance remains the same. Initial Disclosure of Terms and Conditions – 12 CFR 1005.7 Financial institutions must provide initial disclosures of the terms and conditions of EFT services before the first EFT is made or at the time the consumer contracts for an EFT service. They must give a summary of various consumer rights under the regulation, including the consumer’s liability for unauthorized EFTs, the types of EFTs the consumer may make, limits on the frequency or dollar amount, fees charged by the financial institution, and the error-resolution procedures. Appendix A to 12 CFR Part 1005 provides model clauses that financial institutions may use to provide the disclosures. Timing of Disclosures. Financial institutions must make the required disclosures at the time a consumer contracts for an electronic fund transfer service or before the first electronic fund transfer is made involving the consumer’s account (12 CFR 1005.7(a)). Disclosures given by a financial institution earlier than the regulation requires (for example, when the consumer opens a checking account) need not be repeated when the consumer later authorizes an electronic check conversion or agrees with a third party to initiate preauthorized transfers to or from the consumer’s account, unless the terms and conditions differ from the previously disclosed term.         # Periodic Statement Requirements Under Regulation E\n\n## 1. General Frequency Requirement\n\nFinancial institutions must send periodic statements:\n- **For each monthly cycle in which an EFT has occurred**, and\n- **At least quarterly** if no EFT has occurred during a cycle [C:12CFR1005_1005.9_chunk_0002] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0703_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n## 2. Required Content of Periodic Statements\n\nFor each EFT made during the cycle, the periodic statement must include, as applicable [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0703_chunk_0001] [C:12CFR1005_1005.9_chunk_0002]:\n\n**Transaction Information (per EFT):**\n- Amount of the transfer (charges imposed at an electronic terminal by the terminal owner/operator may be included in the amount)\n- Date the transfer was posted to the account\n- Type of transfer(s) and type of account(s) to or from which funds were transferred\n- For each transfer (except deposits of cash or check/draft/similar paper instrument to the consumer's account) initiated at an electronic terminal: the terminal location as required for receipts under 12 CFR 1005.9(a)(5)\n- Name of any third-party payee or payor\n\n**Account-Level Information:**\n- Account number(s) [C:12CFR1005_1005.9_chunk_0002]\n- Total amount of any fees and charges (other than a finance charge as defined by Regulation Z) assessed during the period for making EFTs, the right to make EFTs, or for account maintenance [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0703_chunk_0001]\n- Balance in the account at the **beginning and close** of the statement period [C:12CFR1005_1005.9_chunk_0002]\n- Address and telephone number to be used by the consumer for inquiries or notice of errors (may appear on an accompanying abbreviated error notice) [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0703_chunk_0001]\n- If the financial institution uses the telephone-notice option under 12 CFR 1005.10(a)(1)(iii): a telephone number the consumer may call to ascertain whether preauthorized transfers to the account have occurred [C:12CFR1005_1005.9_chunk_0002]\n\n---\n\n## 3. Exceptions to the Periodic Statement Requirement\n\n### a. Passbook Accounts\nWhere a consumer's passbook account may **only** be accessed by preauthorized transfers to the account, a periodic statement need not be sent, **provided** the financial institution either:\n- Updates the passbook upon presentation (listing the amount and date of each EFT since the passbook was last presented), **or**\n- Provides the required information on a separate document at the consumer's request [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0704_chunk_0001] [C:12CFR1005_1005.9_chunk_0002].\n\n### b. Other Accounts Accessed Only by Preauthorized Transfers\nFor accounts (other than passbook accounts) that may be accessed **only** by preauthorized transfers to the account, the financial institution must send a periodic statement **at least quarterly** [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0704_chunk_0001] [C:12CFR1005_1005.9_chunk_0002].\n\n### c. Intra-Institutional Transfers\nIf an EFT is initiated by the consumer between **two accounts of the consumer at the same financial institution**, documenting the transfer on a periodic statement for **one** of the two accounts satisfies the periodic statement requirement [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0704_chunk_0001] [C:12CFR1005_1005.9_chunk_0002].\n\n> **Note:** An account accessed by both preauthorized transfers to the account and intra-institutional transfers, but by no other type of EFT, qualifies for the preauthorized-transfer exception (not the intra-institutional exception) [C:12CFR1005_1005.9_chunk_0002].\n\n### d. Foreign-Initiated Transfers\nIf an EFT is **initiated outside the United States**, the financial institution need not provide a receipt or a periodic statement reflecting the transfer, **provided** it treats any inquiry for clarification or documentation as a notice of error under 12 CFR 1005.11 [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0704_chunk_0001] [C:12CFR1005_1005.9_chunk_0002].\n\n---\n\n## 4. Alternative to Periodic Statements for Payroll Card Accounts (12 CFR 1005.18)\n\nA financial institution offering **payroll card accounts** need not furnish periodic statements under 12 CFR 1005.9(b) if it makes available to the consumer all of the following [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0704_chunk_0002] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0705_chunk_0001]:\n\n1. The **account balance**, through a readily available telephone line\n2. An **electronic history** of account transactions covering at least **60 days** preceding the date the consumer electronically accesses the account\n3. A **written history** of account transactions provided promptly in response to an oral or written request, covering at least **60 days** preceding the date the financial institution receives the consumer's request\n\nThe history of account transactions must include the same type of information required on periodic statements under 12 CFR 1005.9(b) [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0705_chunk_0001].\n\n### Compliance Obligations When Using the Payroll Card Alternative:\n- **Modify initial disclosures** under 12 CFR 1005.7(b) to disclose: the telephone number for balance inquiries, the means to obtain electronic account history, and a summary of the right to receive a written account history upon request [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0705_chunk_0001]\n- **Provide an annual error resolution notice** substantially similar to the model notice in Appendix A, paragraph A-7(b), in place of the standard annual notice under 12 CFR 1005.8(b) [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0705_chunk_0001]\n- **Liability limits:** For purposes of 12 CFR 1005.6(b)(3), the 60-day period for reporting unauthorized transfers begins on the earlier of the date the consumer electronically accesses the account (if the electronic history reflects the transfer) or the date the written history is provided [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0705_chunk_0001]\n\n---\n\n## 5. Alternative to Periodic Statements for Prepaid Accounts (12 CFR 1005.18 / Prepaid Rule)\n\nFor **prepaid accounts**, a financial institution need not furnish periodic statements under 12 CFR 1005.9(b) if it makes available [C:12CFR1005_1005.18_chunk_0020]:\n\n1. The consumer's **account balance** through a readily available telephone line\n2. An **electronic history** of account transactions covering at least **12 months** preceding the date the consumer electronically accesses the account\n3. A **written history** of account transactions provided promptly upon oral or written request, covering at least **24 months** preceding the date the financial institution receives the request\n\n> **Exception                                                                                                                                           [{"chunk_id": "exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0704_chunk_0001", "source": "exam_manual_v2_2012.pdf", "page": "", "rrf_score": 0.03278688524590164, "text": "CFPB Consumer Laws and Regulations EFTA • If the financial institution has provided a telephone number which the consumer can use to find out whether or not a preauthorized transfer has taken place, that telephone number. Exceptions to the Periodic Statement Requirement for Certain Accounts • Passbook accounts. Where a consumer’s passbook may not be accessed by an EFT other than preauthorized transfers to the account, a periodic statement need not be sent, provided that the financial institution updates the consumer’s passbook or provides the required information on a separate document at the consumer’s request. To update the passbook, the amount and date of each EFT made since the passbook was last presented must be listed (12 CFR 1005.9(c)(1)(i)). For other accounts that may be accessed only by preauthorized transfers to the account, the financial institution must send a periodic statement at least quarterly (12 CFR 1005.9(c)(1)(ii)). • Transfers between accounts. If a transfer occurs between two accounts of the consumer at the same financial institution, the transfer need only be documented for one of the two accounts (12 CFR 1005.9(c)(2)). A preauthorized transfer between two accounts of the consumer at the same financial institution is subject to the 12 CFR 1005.9(c)(1) rule on preauthorized transfers and not the 12 CFR 1005.9(c)(2) rule on intra-institutional transfers (12 CFR 1005.9(c)(3)). • Documentation for Foreign-initiated transfers. If an EFT is initiated outside the United States, the financial institution need not provide a receipt or a periodic statement reflecting the transfer if it treats an inquiry for clarification or documentation as a notice of error (12 CFR 1005.9(d)). Alternatives to Periodic Statements for Financial Institutions Offering Payroll Card Accounts – 12 CFR 1005.18 This section provides an alternative to providing periodic statements for payroll card accounts if financial institutions make the account information available to consumers by specific means. In addition, this section clarifies how financial institutions that do not provide periodic statements for payroll card accounts can comply with the Regulation E requirements relating to initial disclosures, the annual error resolution notice, liability limits, and the error resolution procedures. Typically, employers and third-party service providers do not meet the definition of a “financial institution” subject to the regulation because they neither (i) hold payroll card accounts nor (ii) issue payroll cards and agree with consumers to provide EFT services in connection with payroll card accounts. However, to the extent an employer or a service provider undertakes either of these functions, it would be deemed a financial institution under the regulation (Comment 1005.18(a)-2). The regulation in this part, known as Regulation E, is issued by the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection (Bureau) pursuant to the Electronic Fund Transfer Act (15 U.S.C. 1693 et seq. ). The information-collection requirements have been approved by the Office of Management and Budget under 44 U.S.C. 3501 et seq. and have been assigned OMB No. 3170-0014. (b) Purpose. This part carries out the purposes of the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, which establishes the basic rights, liabilities, and responsibilities of consumers who use electronic fund transfer and remittance transfer services and of financial institutions or other persons that offer these services. # Periodic Statement Requirements Under Regulation E (12 CFR 1005.9)\n\n## 1. General Frequency Requirement\nFinancial institutions must send periodic statements for each monthly cycle in which an EFT has occurred, and at least quarterly if no EFT has occurred during a cycle (12 CFR 1005.9(b)).\n\n## 2. Required Content of Periodic Statements\nFor each EFT made during the cycle, the statement must include, as applicable (12 CFR 1005.9(b); exam manual):\n- Amount of the transfer (a terminal-owner/operator charge imposed at an electronic terminal may be included in the amount);\n- Date the transfer was posted to the account;\n- Type of transfer(s) and type of account(s) to or from which funds were transferred;\n- For each transfer (except deposits of cash, or a check/draft/similar paper instrument to the consumer's account) initiated at an electronic terminal, the terminal location as required for receipts under 1005.9(a)(5);\n- Name of any third-party payee or payor;\n- Account number(s);\n- Total amount of any fees and charges (other than a finance charge under Regulation Z) assessed during the period for making EFTs, the right to make EFTs, or for account maintenance;\n- Balance in the account at the beginning and close of the statement period;\n- Address and telephone number for inquiries or notice of errors (the address/telephone number on an error-resolution notice given on or with the statement satisfies this);\n- If the institution uses the telephone-notice option under 1005.10(a)(1)(iii), a telephone number the consumer may call to ascertain whether preauthorized transfers to the account have occurred.\n\n## 3. Exceptions to the Periodic Statement Requirement (1005.9(c)-(d))\n- **Passbook accounts** accessible only by preauthorized transfers to the account: no periodic statement needed if the institution updates the passbook upon presentation (listing amount and date of each EFT since last presented) or enters the information on a separate document (1005.9(c)(1)(i)).\n- **Other accounts** accessible only by preauthorized transfers to the account: statement required at least quarterly (1005.9(c)(1)(ii)).\n- **Intra-institutional transfers** between two accounts of the consumer at the same institution: documenting the transfer on a periodic statement for one of the two accounts satisfies the requirement (1005.9(c)(2)).\n- An account accessed only by preauthorized transfers to the account and intra-institutional transfers (and no other EFT type) qualifies for the preauthorized-transfer exception under (c)(1) (1005.9(c)(3)).\n- **Foreign-initiated transfers**: no receipt or periodic statement needed if the transfer is not initiated within a state and the institution treats any inquiry for clarification or documentation as a notice of error under 1005.11 (1005.9(d)).\n\n## 4. Payroll Card Account Alternative (12 CFR 1005.18(b))\nAn institution offering payroll card accounts need not furnish periodic statements under 1005.9(b) if it makes available:\n1. The account balance through a readily available telephone line;\n2. An electronic history covering at least 60 days preceding the date the consumer electronically accesses the account;\n3. A written history provided promptly on oral or written request covering at least 60 days preceding the request.\nThe histories must include the same information required on periodic statements under 1005.9(b). The institution must also modify initial disclosures under 1005.7(b), provide a substitute annual error-resolution notice (in place of 1005.8(b)), and apply the 60-day liability-reporting period for 1005.6(b)(3) beginning on the earlier of the date the consumer electronically accesses the account (if the history reflects the transfer) or the date the written history is provided.\n\n## 5. Prepaid Account Alternative (12 CFR 1005.18(c))\nAn institution need not furnish periodic statements under 1005.9(b) for prepaid accounts if it makes available:\n1. The account balance through a readily available telephone line;\n2. An electronic history covering at least 12 months preceding the date the consumer electronically accesses the account;\n3. A written history provided promptly on oral or written request covering at least 24 months preceding the request.\nThe histories must include the information set forth in 1005.9(b). Additionally:\n- For prepaid accounts that are not payroll card or government benefit accounts, the written history under (c)(1)(iii) is not required for any account for which the institution has not completed its consumer identification and verification process (1005.18(c)(2)).\n- The institution must disclose the amount of any fees assessed (whether for EFTs or otherwise) on any periodic statement and on any transaction history (1005.18(c)(4)).\n- The institution must display a summary total of all fees assessed for the prior calendar month and for the calendar year to date on any periodic statement and transaction history (1005.18(c)(5)).\n- The institution must comply with the modified disclosure requirements under 1005.18(d).\n\n(Note: Receipts, as distinct from periodic statements, are not required for EFTs of $15 or less under 1005.9(e).) us.anthropic.claude-opus-4-8 LLM_JUDGE_REVIEWED
      G3-05                                 What constitutes a billing error on an open-end credit account, and what must a creditor do after receiving a proper billing-error notice? ["12 CFR 1026.13"]                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               ["12CFR1005_1005.33_chunk_0005", "12CFR1026_1026.6_chunk_0002", "12CFR1026_1026.6_chunk_0011", "12CFR1026_1026.8_chunk_0001", "12CFR1026_1026.12_chunk_0003", "12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0001", "12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0002", "12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0003", "12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0004", "12CFR1026_1026.54_chunk_0001", "exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0140_chunk_0001", "exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0423_chunk_0001", "exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0478_chunk_0001", "exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0485_chunk_0001"]        NaN ## Billing Errors on Open-End Credit Accounts: Definition and Creditor Obligations\n\n### I. What Constitutes a Billing Error\n\nUnder 12 CFR § 1026.13(a), a **billing error** on an open-end credit account means any of the following seven categories [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0001]:\n\n1. **Unauthorized extension of credit** — A charge reflected on or with a periodic statement for an extension of credit not made to the consumer or to a person with actual, implied, or apparent authority to use the consumer's credit card or open-end credit plan.\n\n2. **Improperly identified transaction** — An extension of credit reflected on or with a periodic statement that is not identified in accordance with the requirements of §§ 1026.7(a)(2) or (b)(2) and 1026.8.\n\n3. **Unaccepted or undelivered goods/services** — An extension of credit reflected on or with a periodic statement for property or services not accepted by the consumer or the consumer's designee, or not delivered to the consumer or the consumer's designee as agreed.\n\n4. **Failure to properly credit a payment** — A reflection on a periodic statement of the creditor's failure to properly credit a payment or other credit issued to the consumer's account.\n\n5. **Computational or accounting error** — A reflection on a periodic statement of a computational or similar error of an accounting nature made by the creditor.\n\n6. **Request for clarification** — A reflection on a periodic statement of an extension of credit for which the consumer requests additional clarification, including documentary evidence.\n\n7. **Failure to deliver a periodic statement** — The creditor's failure to mail or deliver a periodic statement to the consumer's last known address, if that address was received by the creditor in writing at least **20 days** before the end of the billing cycle for which the statement was required. [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0001]\n\n---\n\n### II. What Constitutes a Proper Billing-Error Notice\n\nA **billing error notice** must meet all three of the following requirements [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0001]:\n\n1. **Timely receipt** — Received by the creditor at the address disclosed under § 1026.7(a)(9) or (b)(9) **no later than 60 days** after the creditor transmitted the first periodic statement reflecting the alleged billing error.\n2. **Account identification** — Enables the creditor to identify the consumer's name and account number.\n3. **Description of error** — To the extent possible, indicates the consumer's belief and reasons for believing a billing error exists, and the type, date, and amount of the error.\n\n---\n\n### III. Creditor's Obligations After Receiving a Proper Billing-Error Notice\n\n#### A. Acknowledgment and Resolution Deadlines\n\n- The creditor must **mail or deliver written acknowledgment** to the consumer **within 30 days** of receiving the billing error notice, unless the creditor has already completed the appropriate resolution procedures within that 30-day period. [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0001]\n- The creditor must **complete the appropriate resolution procedures within 2 complete billing cycles, but in no event later than 90 days**, after receiving the billing error notice. [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0001]\n\n#### B. Rules Pending Resolution\n\nUntil the billing error is resolved, the following protections apply [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0002]:\n\n1. **No collection of disputed amount** — The consumer need not pay, and the creditor may not try to collect, any portion of any required payment the consumer believes is related to the disputed amount (including related finance or other charges). For automatic payment plans, the card issuer shall not deduct any part of the disputed amount or related finance or other charges if a billing error notice is received any time up to **3 business days** before the scheduled payment date.\n\n2. **No adverse credit reports** — The creditor or its agent shall not (directly or indirectly) make or threaten to make an adverse report to any person about the consumer's credit standing, or report that an amount or account is delinquent, because the consumer failed to pay the disputed amount or related finance or other charges.\n\n3. **No acceleration or account restriction** — A creditor shall not accelerate any part of the consumer's indebtedness or restrict or close a consumer's account solely because the consumer has exercised in good faith rights provided by this section. A creditor may be subject to the forfeiture penalty under 15 U.S.C. 1666(e) for failure to comply with any of the requirements of this section.\n\n4. **Permitted creditor actions** — The creditor is not prohibited from: collecting any undisputed portion; deducting the disputed amount and related finance or other charges from the consumer's credit limit; or reflecting the disputed amount on a periodic statement, provided the creditor indicates on or with the periodic statement that payment of the disputed amount and related finance or other charges is not required pending the creditor's compliance with this section.\n\n#### C. Resolution Procedures: If Billing Error Occurred as Asserted\n\nIf the creditor determines a billing error occurred as asserted, within the time limits of § 1026.13(c)(2), the creditor shall [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0002]:\n\n1. **Correct the billing error** and credit the consumer's account with any disputed amount and related finance or other charges, as applicable; and\n2. **Mail or deliver a correction notice** to the consumer.\n\n#### D. Resolution Procedures: If No Billing Error or a Different Billing Error Occurred\n\nIf, after conducting a reasonable investigation, the creditor determines no billing error occurred or that a different billing error occurred, within the time limits of § 1026.13(c)(2), the creditor shall [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0003]:\n\n1. **Mail or deliver an explanation** setting forth the reasons for the creditor's belief that the alleged billing error is incorrect in whole or in part;\n2. **Furnish copies of documentary evidence** of the consumer's indebtedness, if the consumer so requests; and\n3. **If a different billing error occurred**, correct that error and credit the consumer's account with any disputed amount and related finance or other charges, as applicable.\n\n#### E. Creditor's Rights and Duties After Resolution\n\nAfter complying with all requirements, if the creditor determines the consumer owes all or part of the disputed amount and related finance or other charges, the creditor [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0003]:\n\n1. **Shall promptly notify the consumer in writing** of the time when payment is due and the portion of the disputed amount and related finance or other charges that the consumer still owes.\n2. **Shall allow any grace period** disclosed under §§ 1026.6(a)(1) or (b)(2)(v) and 1026.7(a)(8) or (b)(8) during which the consumer can pay without incurring additional finance or other charges.\n3. **May report the account as delinquent** only after allowing the disclosed grace period or **10 days** (whichever is longer) for the consumer to pay.\n4. **May not report delinquency** if it receives further written notice from the consumer (within the allowed payment period under § 1026.13(g)(3)) that any portion of the billing error is still in dispute, **unless** the creditor also:\n   - Promptly reports that the amount or account is **in dispute**;\n   - Mails or delivers to the consumer (at the same time the report is made) a **written notice of the name and address** of each person to whom the report is made; and\n   - **Promptly reports any subsequent resolution** of the reported delinquency to all persons to whom the creditor made a report. [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0003] [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0004]\n\n---\n\n### IV. Reassertion of Billing Error (§ 1026.13(h))\n\nUnder 12 CFR § 1026.13(h), a creditor that has **fully complied** with all of the requirements of § 1026.13 has **no further responsibilities** under this section — other than as provided in § 1026.13(g)(4) (which governs the conditions under which a creditor may report a delinquency when the consumer reasserts a dispute within the allowed payment period) — if a consumer **reasserts substantially the same billing error**. [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0004]\n\n---\n\n### V. Relation to the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E (§ 1026.13(i))\n\n#### A. Regulatory Text: When Regulation E Governs Instead of Regulation Z\n\nUnder 12 CFR § 1026.13(i), a creditor shall comply with the error-resolution requirements of **Regulation E** — specifically 12 CFR 1005.11 and, as applicable, 12 CFR 1005.18(e) — **rather than** the Regulation Z provisions in **§ 1026.13(a), (b), (c), (e), (f), and (h)** in the following two circumstances [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0004]:\n\n1. **Overdraft and minimum-balance credit lines** — Except with respect to a prepaid account as defined in § 1026.61, an extension of credit that is incident to an electronic fund transfer occurs under an agreement between the consumer and a financial institution to extend credit when the consumer's account is overdrawn or to maintain a specified minimum balance in the consumer's account.\n\n2. **Hybrid prepaid-credit cards** — With regard to a covered separate credit feature and an asset feature of a prepaid account where both are accessible by a hybrid prepaid-credit card as defined in § 1026.61, an extension of credit that is incident to an electronic fund transfer occurs when the hybrid prepaid-credit card accesses both funds in the asset feature of the prepaid account and a credit extension from the credit feature with respect to a particular transaction.\n\nThe regulation specifies that paragraphs **(a), (b), (c), (e), (f), and (h)** of § 1026.13 are displaced in these circumstances. The regulation does not state that paragraphs (d) and (g) of § 1026.13 are displaced. [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0004]\n\n#### B. Regulation E Error-Resolution Procedures That Apply\n\nWhen Regulation E governs, the following requirements apply under 12 CFR 1005.11:\n\n**Definition of "error" under Regulation E.** Under 12 CFR 1005.11(a)(1), an error includes: an unauthorized EFT; an incorrect EFT to or from the consumer's account; the omission from a periodic statement of an EFT that should have been included; a computational or bookkeeping error made by the financial institution relating to an EFT; the consumer's receipt of an incorrect amount of money from an electronic terminal; an EFT not identified in accordance with the requirements of 12 CFR 1005.9 or 1005.10(a); and a consumer's request for documentation required by 12 CFR 1005.9 or 1005.10(a) or for additional information or clarification concerning an EFT. The term "error" does not include a routine inquiry about the account balance or a request for duplicate copies of documentation made only for tax or other recordkeeping purposes, or the fact that a financial institution does not make a terminal receipt available for a transfer of $15 or less. [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0700_chunk_0001]\n\n**Notice of error.** A financial institution must comply with the Regulation E error-resolution procedures with respect to any oral or written notice of error from the consumer that: (1) is received no later than 60 days after the financial institution sends a periodic statement or other documentation first reflecting the alleged error; (2) enables the financial institution to identify the consumer's name and account number; and (3) indicates why the consumer believes the error exists and, to the extent possible, the type, date, and amount of the error. A financial institution may require a consumer to give written confirmation of an error within 10 business days of giving oral notice, and must provide the address where confirmation must be sent. [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0700_chunk_0001]\n\n**Investigation and resolution timelines.** After receiving a notice of error, the financial institution must promptly investigate and, under the standard 10-business-day period, determine whether an error occurred within 10 business days of receiving the notice, report the results to the consumer within three business days after completing its investigation, and correct the error within one business day after determining that an error occurred. [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0700_chunk_0001] [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002]\n\nIf the financial institution is unable to complete its investigation within 10 business days, it may take up to 45 days from receipt of the notice to investigate, provided it: (i) provisionally credits the consumer's account in the amount of the alleged error (including interest where applicable) within 10 business days of receiving the error notice (with a permissible withholding of up to $50 if the institution has a reasonable basis for believing an unauthorized EFT occurred and has satisfied the requirements of § 1005.6(a)); (ii) informs the consumer within two business days after the provisional crediting of the amount and date of the provisional credit and gives the consumer full use of the funds during the investigation; (iii) corrects the error, if any, within one business day after determining that an error occurred; and (iv) reports the results to the consumer within three business days after completing its investigation, including notice that a provisional credit has been made final if applicable. [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002]\n\nThe 10-business-day and 45-day periods are extended in certain circumstances: the applicable time is 20 business days in place of 10 business days if the notice of error involves an EFT to or from the account within 30 days after the first deposit to the account was made; and the applicable time is 90 days in place of 45 days for completing an investigation if the notice of error involves an EFT that was not initiated within a state, resulted from a point-of-sale debit card transaction, or occurred within 30 days after the first deposit to the account was made. [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002]\n\nThe provisional-credit requirement does not apply if the institution requires but does not receive written confirmation within 10 business days of an oral notice of error, or if the alleged error involves an account subject to Regulation T of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System.       G3-01 After a consumer notifies a financial institution of an electronic fund transfer error, what investigation and resolution steps are required, and within what time limits?                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           # Electronic Fund Transfer Error Investigation and Resolution Requirements\n\n## 1. Triggering a Valid Notice of Error\n\nA financial institution must comply with error resolution procedures when it receives an oral or written notice of error that [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0001]:\n\n- Is received **no later than 60 days** after the institution sends the periodic statement on which the alleged error is first reflected;\n- Enables the institution to identify the **consumer's name and account number**; and\n- Indicates **why the consumer believes an error exists**, including to the extent possible the type, date, and amount of the error.\n\nThe institution may require the consumer to provide **written confirmation within 10 business days** of an oral notice. If it does, it must inform the consumer of this requirement and provide the address for sending confirmation [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n## 2. Standard Investigation Timeline: 10-Business-Day Period\n\nAfter receiving a valid notice of error, the financial institution must [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002]:\n\n1. **Investigate promptly** and determine whether an error occurred **within 10 business days** of receiving the notice.\n2. **Report results to the consumer within 3 business days** after completing the investigation.\n3. **Correct the error within 1 business day** after determining that an error occurred.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Extended Investigation Timeline: 45-Calendar-Day Period\n\nIf the institution **cannot complete its investigation within 10 business days**, it may take **up to 45 days** from receipt of the notice, provided it does **all** of the following [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002]:\n\n1. **Provisionally credits** the consumer's account in the full amount of the alleged error (including interest where applicable) **within 10 business days** of receiving the error notice.\n   - If the institution has a reasonable basis for believing an unauthorized EFT occurred and has satisfied § 1005.6(a) requirements, it may **withhold up to $50** from the provisional credit.\n2. **Informs the consumer within 2 business days** after the provisional crediting of the amount and date of the credit, and gives the consumer **full use of the funds** during the investigation.\n3. **Corrects the error within 1 business day** after determining that an error occurred.\n4. **Reports results to the consumer within 3 business days** after completing the investigation, including notice that a provisional credit has been made final (if applicable).\n\n### Exceptions — No Provisional Credit Required:\nThe institution need **not** provisionally credit the account (and thus may still take up to 45 days) if [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002]:\n- The institution required but **did not receive written confirmation** within 10 business days of an oral notice; **or**\n- The alleged error involves an account subject to **Regulation T** (Securities Credit by Brokers and Dealers, 12 CFR Part 220).\n\n---\n\n## 4. Further Extended Time Periods\n\nCertain circumstances extend the standard deadlines [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0702_chunk_0001]:\n\n| Circumstance | Standard Period | Extended Period |\n|---|---|---|\n| EFT occurred within **30 days after first deposit** to the account | 10 business days | **20 business days** |\n| EFT occurred within **30 days after first deposit** (45-day extended period) | 45 days | **90 days** |\n| EFT **not initiated within a state** | 45 days | **90 days** |\n| EFT resulted from a **point-of-sale debit card transaction** | 45 days | **90 days** |\n\n---\n\n## 5. Scope of Investigation\n\nA financial institution's review of **its own records** satisfies the investigation requirement if [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0003]:\n- The alleged error concerns a transfer **to or from a third party**; **and**\n- There is **no agreement** between the institution and the third party for the type of EFT involved.\n\nHowever, the institution **may not limit its investigation solely to payment instructions** where other records pertaining to the account may help resolve the consumer's claim [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0701_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n## 6. The financial institution may take up to 45 calendar days (12 CFR 1005.11(c)(2)) to complete its investigation provided it: • Provisionally credits the funds (including interest, where applicable) to the consumer’s account within the 10 business-day period. • Advises the consumer within two business days of the provisional crediting. • Gives the consumer full use of the funds during the investigation. However, where an error involves an unauthorized EFT, the financial institution must comply with the requirements of the provisions relating to unauthorized EFTs before holding the consumer liable, even if the consumer does not provide a notice of error within the time limits in 12 CFR 1005.11(b) (Comment 1005.11(b)(1)-7). When investigating a claim of error, the financial institution need only review its own records if the alleged error concerns a transfer to or from a third party, and there is no agreement between the financial institution and the third party for the type of EFT involved (12 CFR 1005.11(c)(4)).                                                                                                                                                             ## Liability Limits for Lost or Stolen Access Devices Under Regulation E\n\n### Threshold Conditions for Any Liability\n\nBefore a consumer can be held liable at all, certain conditions must be satisfied. Under 12 CFR 1005.6(a), a consumer may be held liable for an unauthorized EFT only if the financial institution has provided the disclosures required by § 1005.7(b)(1), (2), and (3) — specifically: a summary of consumer liability, the telephone number and address for reporting, and the institution's business days. If the unauthorized transfer involved an access device, it must be an **accepted** access device, and the financial institution must have provided **a means to identify** the consumer to whom the device was issued [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\nRegulation E expressly **prohibits** using consumer negligence (e.g., writing a PIN on an ATM card) or a deposit agreement as a basis for imposing greater liability than the limits set forth in § 1005.6(b). The extent of the consumer's liability is determined solely by the consumer's promptness in notifying the financial institution [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0697_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### Tiered Liability Structure for Loss or Theft of an Access Device\n\nThe first two tiers under 12 CFR 1005.6(b)(1) and (b)(2) apply **only when an access device is lost or stolen**. They do not apply to unauthorized transfers made without an access device (see the separate rule below) [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0728_chunk_0001].\n\n#### Tier 1 — § 1005.6(b)(1): Notice Given Within Two Business Days of Learning of Loss or Theft\n\n- **Maximum liability:** The **lesser of $50** or the total amount of unauthorized transfers that occur before notice is given to the financial institution [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\nPer CFPB examination checklist guidance, examiners verify that the institution limits liability to this amount when the consumer notifies within the two-business-day window [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0727_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n#### Tier 2 — § 1005.6(b)(2): Notice NOT Given Within Two Business Days (but within 60 calendar days of statement transmittal)\n\n- **Maximum liability:** The **lesser of $500** or the **sum of**:\n  - (a) $50 **or** the amount of unauthorized transfers occurring within the first two business days, **whichever is less**; **AND**\n  - (b) The amount of unauthorized transfers occurring **after** the close of two business days and **before** notice to the institution — *provided the institution establishes that these transfers would not have occurred had the consumer notified the institution within the two-day period* [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\nPer CFPB examination checklist guidance, examiners verify that the institution does not exceed this cap when the consumer fails to notify within two business days [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0727_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n#### Tier 3 — § 1005.6(b)(3): Failure to Report Within 60 Calendar Days of Periodic Statement Transmittal\n\nThis rule applies to **all** unauthorized EFTs appearing on a periodic statement — whether or not an access device was involved — and operates separately from Tiers 1 and 2 [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\nUnder 12 CFR 1005.6(b)(3), a consumer must report an unauthorized electronic fund transfer that appears on a periodic statement **within 60 calendar days** of the institution's transmittal of that statement to avoid liability for subsequent transfers. If the consumer **fails** to do so, the consumer's liability shall not exceed the amount of unauthorized transfers occurring **after** the close of the 60-day period and **before** notice to the institution, provided the institution establishes that those transfers would not have occurred had timely notice been given [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\nWhen an **access device** is involved in the unauthorized transfer, the consumer may **also** be liable for amounts set forth in § 1005.6(b)(1) or (b)(2), as applicable [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\n**Late reporting when an access device is involved — distinction between transfer timing:** CFPB examination guidance further clarifies that when a consumer reports more than 60 calendar days after transmittal of the statement showing the first unauthorized transfer made with an access device, the liability analysis distinguishes between two categories of transfers:\n\n- For unauthorized transfers occurring **within** the 60-day period: liability is capped at the lesser of $500, or the sum of (a) the lesser of $50 or the amount of unauthorized transfers in the first two business days, and (b) the amount of unauthorized transfers occurring after two business days (subject to the institution's burden of proof); and\n- For unauthorized transfers occurring **after** the 60-day period: the consumer faces **unlimited liability** until the financial institution is notified, provided the institution demonstrates those transfers would not have occurred had timely notice been given [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001].\n\nCFPB examination checklist guidance confirms: if the consumer notifies within 60 days, the institution may not hold the consumer liable for transfers occurring after the 60-day period; if the consumer does not notify within 60 days, liability is limited to transfers occurring after the 60-day period and before notice, subject to the institution's burden of proof [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0728_chunk_0001].\n\n> **Important distinction (CFPB examination checklist guidance):** The first two tiers of liability under § 1005.6(b)(1) and (b)(2) do **not** apply to unauthorized transfers from a consumer's account made **without** an access device. Only the 60-day rule under § 1005.6(b)(3) governs such transfers [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0728_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### Special Rule: Unauthorized Transfers NOT Involving an Access Device\n\nWhere an unauthorized transfer occurs **without** the loss or theft of an access device (e.g., account number compromise without a card), the tiered $50/$500 structure of § 1005.6(b)(1) and (b)(2) does **not** apply. Instead, only the 60-day periodic statement rule under § 1005.6(b)(3) governs. CFPB examination guidance summarizes the outcomes for this scenario as follows:\n\n| Timing of Consumer Notice | Maximum Liability |\n|---|---|\n| Within 60 calendar days after transmittal of the periodic statement on which the unauthorized transfer first appears | No liability for unauthorized transfers occurring after the 60-day period |\n| More than 60 calendar days after transmittal of the periodic statement on which the unauthorized transfer first appears | Unlimited liability for unauthorized transfers occurring after the 60-day period and before notice to the financial institution (provided the institution establishes the transfers would not have occurred had timely notice been given) |\n\n[C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0728_chunk_0001]\n\nNote that the "no liability" characterization in the table above reflects CFPB examination guidance summarizing the practical outcome; the text of 12 CFR 1005.6(b)(3) itself frames the rule in terms of what liability the consumer incurs for transfers occurring *after* the close of the 60-day period [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### Extension of Time Limits for Extenuating Circumstances\n\nIf the consumer's delay in notifying the financial institution was due to **extenuating circumstances** (e.g., extended travel or hospitalization), the institution **must extend** the applicable time periods — including the two-business-day and 60-day periods — to a **reasonable period** [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0699_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### How Notice Is Given\n\n- Notice is effective when the consumer **takes steps reasonably necessary** to provide the institution with pertinent information, whether or not a particular employee actually receives it [C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001].\n- At the consumer's option, notice may be given **in person, by telephone, or in writing** [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0699_chunk_0001].\n- Written notice is considered given at the time of mailing or delivery for transmission [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0699_chunk_0001].\n- Notice may also be considered given when the institution becomes aware of circumstances leading to a reasonable belief that an unauthorized transfer has been or may be made [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0699_chunk_0001].\n- The consumer need not provide the account or card number; sufficiently identifying the account (e.g., name and account type) is enough [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0699_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### Special Rule: Service Providers Without Account-Holding Agreements\n\nWhere a service provider issues a debit card but does not hold the consumer's account and has no agreement with the account-holding institution, the **two-business-day notice period under § 1005.6(b)(1) and (b)(2) is extended to four business days**, and the **60-day reporting period under § 1005.6(b)(3) is extended to 90 days** [C:12CFR1005_1005.14_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### Reduced Liability by Agreement or State Law\n\nA financial institution **may impose less** consumer liability than the statutory limits based on state law or the deposit agreement [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001].\n\n---\n\n### Summary Table\n\n| Scenario | Timing of Consumer Notice | Maximum Liability |\n|---|---|---|\n| Loss/theft of access device — § 1005.6(b)(1) | Within 2 business days of learning of loss/theft | Lesser of **$50** or actual unauthorized transfers before notice |\n| Loss/theft of access device — § 1005.6(b)(2) | More than 2 business days after learning of loss/theft, up to 60 days after statement | Lesser of **$500** or sum of (a) lesser of $50 or transfers in first 2 days, plus (b) transfers after 2 days and before notice (institution must prove causation) |\n| Loss/theft of access device — more than 60 days after statement | More than 60 calendar days after transmittal of statement showing first unauthorized transfer | For transfers within the 60-day period: lesser of $500 per (b)(2) calculation; for transfers after the 60-day period: **unlimited** (until notice; institution must prove causation) |\n| Any unauthorized EFT on periodic statement — § 1005.6(b)(3) (access device or not) | Within 60 calendar days after statement transmittal | **No additional liability** for post-60-day transfers |\n| Any unauthorized EFT on periodic statement — § 1005.6(b)(3) (access device or not) | More than 60 calendar days after statement transmittal | **Unlimited** for transfers after the 60-day period and before notice (institution must prove causation); if access device involved, also subject to (b)(1)/(b)(2) amounts for transfers within the 60-day period |\n| Unauthorized transfer **without** access device | Within 60 days of statement | No liability for post-60-day transfers (per CFPB examination guidance) |\n| Unauthorized transfer **without** access device | More than 60 days after statement | Unlimited for post-60-day transfers and before notice (institution must prove causation) |\n\n[C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0728_chunk_0001]                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       [{"chunk_id": "exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001", "source": "exam_manual_v2_2012.pdf", "page": "", "rrf_score": 0.03252247488101534, "text": "CFPB Consumer Laws and Regulations EFTA those time limits, are listed in the chart below.
